subject: Computer Networking
title: HTTP/2 and Multiplexing
description: A micro-lesson that makes HTTP/2 and Multiplexing usable.

hook.text: Web pages need dozens of files: HTML, CSS, JS, images. HTTP/1.1 loaded them mostly one at a time.

buildup.text: HTTP/2 introduced multiplexing — many requests and responses travel over a single TCP connection.

discovery.text: Streams are interleaved. While waiting for a big image, smaller CSS files slip through the same connection.

twist.text: HTTP/2 also compresses headers and allows server push — sending resources before the browser asks.

climax.text: Most major websites run on HTTP/2 today. Users don't see it, but pages load noticeably faster.

punchline.text: HTTP/2 sends more through less. One connection, many streams.

quiz.question: What is multiplexing in HTTP/2?
options: Sending multiple requests over a single connection simultaneously
Splitting a file into packets for faster delivery

details.summary: HTTP/2 introduced binary framing, multiplexing, header compression, and server push to dramatically improve web performance over HTTP/1.1. Multiplexing allows multiple requests and responses to share a single TCP connection simultaneously, eliminating the head-of-line blocking problem.
details.whyItMatters: HTTP/2 doubled web page loading speed for many sites by eliminating the inefficiencies of HTTP/1.1's serial request model. It is now the default protocol for the majority of web traffic.
takeaways: Multiplexing sends multiple requests over one TCP connection
Header compression with HPACK reduces overhead significantly
Binary framing replaces text-based HTTP/1.1 for efficiency

faq.question: What is head-of-line blocking?
faq.answer: In HTTP/1.1, requests on a single connection are processed sequentially. A slow response blocks all subsequent requests. HTTP/2 multiplexing interleaves request and response frames so a slow resource does not block others. However, TCP-level head-of-line blocking can still occur with packet loss.

faq.question: Does HTTP/2 require HTTPS?
faq.answer: The HTTP/2 specification allows unencrypted connections, but all major browsers only support HTTP/2 over TLS. In practice, you need a valid HTTPS certificate to use HTTP/2 in browsers. This effectively made TLS mandatory for modern web performance.
